bjorn.name: Chairman Bjørn
bjorn.start: Welcome! We have a small gig at Kryptonitt. The rest you'll have to win yourself.
bjorn.inCredit: We're living on the credit line now. The bank sends Christmas cards, but not the nice kind.
bjorn.heat: I don't want to know what you're up to. But be careful.
bjorn.overworked: People are working too much. Good for this quarter, bad for the next.
bjorn.bench: Too many people on the bench. Win something, or rethink the staffing.
bjorn.losing: We're losing money. That's not a strategy.
bjorn.growing: We're growing. Remember people need to be happy too.
bjorn.fine: Steady as she goes. The board is pleased, meaning me.
bjorn.endLost: It didn't work out this time. The next company will be better.
bjorn.endGreat: Impressive. I'll take the credit at the next board meeting.
bjorn.endOk: A proper company. That's more than most manage.

salaryHints.low: Below market. Cheap now, expensive later.
salaryHints.high: Above market. People stay, and headhunters give up.

culture.explain: Budgets apply to all {{hc}} employees. Engineering culture wins tenders and brings in stronger hires. Social culture keeps people. Both build up over time.

tenders.title: Tender board
tenders.intro: Tenders are decided at the end of their deadline quarter and start the quarter after. Green seats you can staff yourself, yellow partly. The rest is covered first by free people from other disciplines (flex, slightly lower rate), then by freelancers. Small gigs (1–2 consultants) appear every quarter. Key tenders (frameworks and big projects) come with a customer meeting and a promise about the start. Routine ones go out as a standard offer with one click.
tenders.freeHint: You'll have {{free}} available when it starts.
tenders.lastChance: Last chance: decided when you end the quarter!
tenders.capacityLine: {{free}} free, {{offered}} of them offered in bids and {{idle}} with no bid. Seats in bids starting next quarter: {{seats}}. Starting later: {{later}}.
tenders.quickBidTooWeak: The customer would turn this offer down. You don't have enough people free, or the CVs are too weak.

bid.noStars: You have no stars to offer yet.

bid.pitchAbandoned: The meeting was cut short. The client noted 0 out of 100.
bid.routineInfo: Routine job: no customer meeting. The customer assumes a perfectly ordinary impression.

needItems.fullTeam: Wants to get going right away. The whole team, ideally yesterday.
needItems.phased: Has been burnt by switching vendors. Wants a calm start and continuity.
needItems.discovery: Wants to understand the problem before committing.
needItems.tightBudget: Tight budget. Price matters a lot.
needItems.concrete: Likes concrete answers with numbers and references.
needItems.visionary: Wants to hear the big picture.
needItems.humble: Tired of overconfident vendors. Values honesty.
needItems.buzzword: Reads a lot of LinkedIn. Likes words like “scalable”.
needItems.styleUnknown: You don't know them well enough yet to tell how they like to be talked to.

bid.promiseHint: The promise follows the contract. After the first quarter, the customer checks whether you kept it.

fullTeam.label: “The whole team is ready.”
fullTeam.con: If you're short of people in the first quarter, the customer is let down.

phased.label: “Two now, the rest next quarter.”
phased.pro: The customer accepts that not everyone is free yet.
phased.con: A little less impressive. If contractors fill more than half the seats, the promise is broken.

discovery.label: “We’ll start with a paid discovery phase.”
discovery.pro: A happier customer and better odds of an extension
discovery.con: The first quarter is billed at half the rate.

minigame.oneShot: You only get one attempt per tender.

contracts.title: Contracts
contracts.none: No active contracts. The tender board awaits.
contracts.explain: Low satisfaction can get you fired. Freelancers, flex and outsourcing drag it down, good people lift it. Happy clients (above 60) often extend.

nurture.title: Client care
nurture.body: Dinner, a workshop and a sincere "so how is it really going?". Adds {{points}} satisfaction, but never above {{max}}. Available every other quarter.
nurture.done: You looked after this client this quarter.

renegotiate.title: Renegotiate the rate
renegotiate.body: Ask for a higher rate: ×{{from}} → ×{{to}}. One try per contract. A yes costs a little satisfaction, a no costs more, and the client remembers.
renegotiate.go: Ask for a new rate ({{chance}} chance)
renegotiate.won: The client agreed to the new rate.
renegotiate.lost: The client said no. There won't be another try on this contract.

upsell.title: Offer more people
upsell.body: Suggest more consultants on the project. They bill from this quarter. A no dents satisfaction slightly, and you have to wait {{quarters}} quarters before trying again.

cancel.title: Cancel the contract
cancel.body: End the contract now. You pay an exit fee of {{fee}}, lose reputation, and your relationship with the client takes a real knock. Your people are free straight away.

market.explain: You're in place {{rank}}. You only see other firms' morale with intel from the backroom.

backroom.title: The Backroom
backroom.intro: This is where things happen that don't make the annual report. Everything has a price, and sometimes you get caught.
backroom.confirm: Are you ABSOLUTELY sure? Your compliance department is one guy called Tor, and he reads everything.
backroom.noStars: They have no stars to steal.
backroom.noOwnBids: You need to place a bid first.
backroom.shareHint: 0% turns outsourcing off. A higher share means more margin and more risk.
backroom.noIntel: You know nothing. Maybe that's for the best.
backroom.intelBids: You can see all bids on the tender from {{customer}}.
backroom.intelFirm: morale {{morale}}, pay {{premium}}% above market, engineering culture {{fag}}, {{hc}} people.

strategy.title: Strategy
strategy.intro: This is where you decide what kind of firm you want to be. The choices give a bonus in tenders that fit.

specialty.title: Specialisation
specialty.hint: Tenders that match your specialisation get +{{sector}} quality for a sector and +{{discipline}} for a discipline. The first choice is free, changing costs {{cost}}.

partners.title: Partnerships
partners.hint: Tenders with seats in the partner's discipline get +{{bonus}} quality. At most {{max}} at a time.

lobby.title: Lobbying
lobby.hint: A round of lunches with every public-sector client: +{{rel}} relationship with each. Once every {{cooldown}} quarters.

departments.title: Departments
departments.hint: Departments cost money every quarter while they are open. You can close them at any time.

acquisitions.title: Acquisitions
acquisitions.hint: You get the people, stars, contracts and client relationships. The old owners keep the cash. The firm can be at most half your size, and the new people are a little less happy at first.
acquisitions.none: No firms of a suitable size right now.
acquisitions.confirm: Buy {{firm}} for {{price}}? There is no undo.

ipo.hint: Sell {{share}} of the firm on the stock exchange and get {{proceeds}} in cash. After that, the valuation counts only the owners’ share, with a small listing premium on the multiple. Every quarter weaker than the last costs reputation and morale. There is no undo.

ipo.confirm: Take {{firm}} public and raise {{proceeds}}? There is no undo, and shareholders will be watching every quarter.

goal.title: Ten years, one quarter at a time
goal.body: You've just founded {{firm}}. You have {{quarters}} quarters, from {{start}} to {{end}}, to build the most valuable consultancy in the country. {{rivals}} other firms have the same idea.
points: Your firm's value is last year's operating profit times a multiple that follows your reputation, plus the cash in the bank.
Whoever is worth the most when time runs out wins.
Stay over your credit limit for too long and the firm goes bankrupt, which ends the game. However nice your slides were.

quarter.title: How a quarter works
quarter.body: Each turn is one quarter. Do as much as you like, then press “{{endTurn}}”. Your rivals make their moves and the books are settled.
points: Post job openings under {{staff}}. Whoever says yes starts the quarter after.
Work you win shows up under {{contracts}}. That's where the money comes from.
The to-do list on the {{dashboard}} shows what needs doing before the quarter ends.

tenders.title: Tenders take time
tenders.body: You can bid on a tender in the quarter it's published and the one after. The client decides at the end of that second quarter, and the work starts the quarter after that.
points: You need enough people in the right disciplines when the work starts, so hire a little ahead.
The customer weighs price against quality. Big tenders and frameworks come with a meeting and a promise about the start. Small jobs go out with one click.
When a contract is about to end, a happy client may renew it.

people.title: You sell people
people.body: Your consultants are the only thing you have to sell. People on the bench cost salary and earn nothing. People who work too hard leave.
points: The capacity panel on the {{dashboard}} shows who's billing and who's on the bench, now and next quarter.
Happy clients build your reputation, and reputation makes the firm worth more.
Morale keeps people around. Replacing a senior takes longer than you think.

ahead.title: What's ahead
ahead.body: The firm goes up a level when you hit any one of the goals for headcount, revenue or tenders won. Every level means a new office, bigger tenders and new options:

onboarding.bjorn: I'm the chair of the board. I'll turn up with advice whenever it suits me. Good luck!

game.title: What is this?
body: Konsulent Tycoon is a turn-based strategy game where you run your own IT consultancy. You have {{quarters}} quarters, from {{start}} to {{end}}, to build the most valuable firm in the country. {{rivals}} rivals have the same idea.

You hire people, bid on tenders, keep clients happy and try not to run out of cash. Whoever has the most valuable firm when time runs out wins. Stay over your credit line for too long and you go bankrupt.

creator.title: Who made it?
body: The game is made by Kristofer Giltvedt Selbekk, who has worked at Bekk since 2013 and is proud of it.

He has always loved tycoon games, especially Transport Tycoon, Theme Hospital and Theme Park, and wanted to make something in the same spirit, set in an industry he knows from the inside. Consulting, after all, is interesting, complex, fun and hard all at once.

satire.title: How much of it is true?
body: Not much. The game plays with common misconceptions and prejudices about what consultancies actually do. Kristofer has never met anything but thoroughly professional people in the industry, but there are plenty of prejudices to have fun with.
Every firm name is made up. If some of them remind you of Kristofer's own employer and its competitors, that's mostly for fun.

making.title: How it was made
body: The game was built with Claude Code, lots of user testing and many rounds of iteration, trial and error, much like every other product Kristofer works on. It took far less time than anything he has built before.
It's still in development, so things may change along the way.

privacy.title: Your data
body: The game is free and runs in your browser. Saved games stay on your own device, and nothing is sent anywhere. Not yet, at least: tracking or a server might come later.

thanks.title: Thanks
body: A big thank you to everyone who has playtested, given feedback along the way and said this reminded them of something they played as a kid.
